strengths: Proposes a novel and conceptually elegant combination of Bayesian cross-validation with data fission/measurement splitting, enabling model evaluation from a single noisy measurement in imaging inverse problems.
The framework is compatible with modern implicit image priors and samplers, including plug-and-play Langevin and diffusion-based posterior samplers, which is a practically important feature.

Introduces two useful scoring rules: a likelihood-based rule for probing likelihood misspecification and a posterior-based embedding rule for prior/OOD detection, with practical Monte Carlo estimators.
Establishes a clear theoretical connection to posterior predictive checks and recovers the marginal likelihood in the limit alpha -> 0, giving useful intuition for the method.

Experimental results are promising across diverse tasks (Gaussian toy example, blind deblurring, natural-image OOD detection, MRI reconstruction, and Poisson noise), showing high selection/detection accuracy with modest sample budgets.
weaknesses: The central claim of being fully unsupervised and requiring only a single noisy measurement is contradicted by the OOD detection experiments, which rely on a reference in-distribution dataset (e.g., 60 FFHQ images, 50 brain scans) to set the 95th-percentile threshold. This undermines the headline claim and limits practical applicability when no such reference measurements are available.

The OOD detection experiments lack comparisons to relevant existing unsupervised/supervised OOD methods (e.g., [48], [31], [18], [14]) despite citing them as related work. The model selection experiment also compares only to the residual-based baseline [55], so claims of excellent performance are not strongly substantiated.

The posterior-based scoring rule Phi2 lacks theoretical grounding: it is not shown to be a proper scoring rule, and its behavior under strong priors, weak likelihoods, or specific misspecification types is not analyzed. It may fail when posterior samples are insensitive to the data or when the embedding is poorly chosen.

The method is evaluated through approximate posterior samplers (DiffPIR, PnP Langevin), so the reported scores may reflect sampler error rather than model misspecification. This important confound is not discussed or controlled.

Key hyperparameters (alpha, K, N, embedding choice for Phi2, detection threshold) are chosen heuristically and appear application-dependent. There is little systematic sensitivity analysis or practical guidance beyond the Gaussian toy example.
The claim of low computational cost is not supported by quantitative runtime or wall-clock comparisons to baselines; only sample counts are reported.
Reproducibility is weakened by missing/blank code and model links in the reproducibility statement, making it impossible to verify the reported experiments.

The manuscript contains several typographical/mathematical presentation issues (e.g., Eq. 3 defines both y+ and y- as f_alpha^-; Eq. 2 has unbalanced parentheses; the supplementary Eq. 14 labels the likelihood terms in a confusing/swapped manner), which hinder clarity.

Limitations are not adequately discussed: the reference-data requirement for OOD detection, dependence on task-specific embeddings, sensitivity to sampler quality, and failure modes are only partially acknowledged.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and well-motivated problem: objective model selection and misspecification/OOD diagnosis for Bayesian imaging when only a single noisy measurement is available and modern learned priors (diffusion, plug-and-play) are used. The motivation that highly informative priors can override the likelihood in ill-posed problems is convincing.

The core idea - combining Bayesian cross-validation / partial predictive checks with data fission (measurement splitting by noise injection) - is a clean and sensible combination that is, to my knowledge, novel in this imaging context, and it is genuinely agnostic to the prior class and compatible with Langevin/PnP and diffusion samplers.

The paper includes an analytical Gaussian analysis (Section 4.1 and SM Section A) that builds useful intuition about the role of the splitting parameter alpha and the number of noise realizations K, including a characterization of the bias introduced by splitting and its reduction with K.

The empirical study is broad in scope: blur-kernel/likelihood selection, natural-image OOD detection with two diffusion priors, MRI reconstruction at two acceleration factors, and a Poisson-noise extension, using two scoring rules (likelihood-based Phi1 and perceptual Phi2).

Reproducibility is taken seriously: code is released and pretrained models/datasets are indicated, and the authors discuss several limitations and edge cases (e.g., the Met-Faces 'limit' case, sensitivity to alpha, and dependence on the embedding used in Phi2).
weaknesses: The central statistical objects are not proper scoring rules, yet the paper leans on Gneiting & Raftery [17] for the notion of strict properness. The authors themselves note that the likelihood rule Phi1 is only 'closely related' to the logarithmic score via Jensen's inequality, and Phi2 is a heuristic perceptual discrepancy between two posteriors rather than a scoring rule. No consistency, identifiability, or 'true model is favored' result is provided, so the theoretical basis for the model-selection claim is thin.

The headline OOD-detection contribution has essentially no baselines. The only quantitative comparison to prior work is Table 1 (kernel selection vs. residuals [55]), which is acknowledged elsewhere to be unreliable [34]. For OOD detection the paper only compares Phi1 against Phi2. It claims to be the first single-measurement OOD method but never compares against the unsupervised diffusion OOD method [48] (whose pretrained priors it actually reuses in the MRI experiment) nor against [31, 18, 58, 14]. This is a serious evidential gap for the main claim.

Evaluation sizes are small and the reported error rates are correspondingly noisy. Type I error and power in Tables 2, 3, 8, 9 are computed over 50-90 images (e.g., 100% power on the 'strong OOD' group, which aggregates only ~30 images across three datasets), so the headline numbers carry wide uncertainty and the null distribution is only empirically calibrated at the 95th percentile.

The 'low computational cost' claim is not substantiated and is questionable. The estimator requires K x N posterior sampling runs per candidate model (K=10, N=20-100, plus diffusion sampling), which for 256x256 images with DiffPIR is substantial and is not obviously cheaper than the marginal-likelihood or nested-sampling alternatives the paper positions itself against. No wall-clock or FLOP comparisons are reported.

Bias from data fission is only partially controlled. The Gaussian analysis (Fig. 11) shows slow convergence and an estimator that has not converged at the sampling budgets used; the authors argue fine convergence is unnecessary but only support this with a few example images. The behavior for non-Gaussian noise and for likelihood-misspecified settings is not characterized, and alpha is chosen by hand (0.1 for natural images, 0.25 for MRI) with no principled selection criterion.

There is a potential circularity that is not addressed: the data-fission split is constructed using the assumed noise model, which is awkward when likelihood misspecification is itself a target of diagnosis. The paper does not discuss how misspecification of the noise model affects the validity of the conditional-independence construction.

The OOD test requires a reference in-distribution set to calibrate the threshold, which weakens the 'only from a single noisy measurement' framing for the OOD application. This dependence on reference data should be stated more explicitly and its cost analyzed.

Presentation is occasionally sloppy: Eq. (3) labels both splits as f_alpha^-(y,w) (the first should be f_alpha^+); Eq. (4) has mismatched parentheses; and there are assorted typos. The connections in Section 3.3 (Eqs. 10-11) are asserted rather than derived in any depth.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated methodological contribution: combining data fission (measurement splitting by noise injection) with Bayesian cross-validation to enable model selection and misspecification testing in imaging inverse problems from a single measurement is a genuinely new and sensible idea that fills a real gap. Existing unsupervised evaluation methods are ill-suited to imaging because of cost and incompatibility with implicit ML priors.

Strong theoretical grounding and analysis: the paper elegantly connects the proposed summary to the marginal likelihood in the α→0 limit and to posterior predictive checks (Eqs. 10-11), providing a principled interpretation. The analytic Gaussian case (Section 4.1, SM A) gives exact formulas and a clear characterization of the accuracy/efficiency trade-off controlled by α and K.

Practicality and compatibility: the method is agnostic to the prior class and works with modern samplers (PnP Langevin/SK-ROCK and DiffPIR diffusion), and it explicitly targets computational efficiency, which is a genuine advantage over nested sampling and marginal-likelihood estimators for high-dimensional imaging.

Two well-chosen scoring rules: a numerically stable likelihood-based rule (Φ1) and a perceptual posterior-based rule (Φ2) with configurable embeddings (identity/LPIPS/CLIP), which the authors correctly argue probe different failure modes (likelihood vs. prior misspecification).

Convincing empirical results across modalities and noise models: 86.7% single-shot and 100% few-shot kernel selection (vs. 40-60% for residual baselines), near-nominal Type I error and high power for OOD detection on natural images, and excellent MRI discrimination, plus a Poisson-noise extension demonstrating generalization beyond Gaussian.

Good reproducibility: code is provided, the SM gives implementation details (sampler settings, kernel definitions, number of steps, valid-padding handling) and honest documentation of borderline failures.

Honest and informative treatment of failure cases: the SM discusses when Φ2 fails (e.g., Met-Faces at high blur, MRI knee model), why LPIPS embeddings trained on natural images underperform on MRI, and where increasing iterations would help.
weaknesses: The model-selection evaluation is limited in scale: only five blur kernels and three test images for kernel selection, and the 'few-shot' setting pools three measurements, which partially relaxes the paper's central 'single measurement' premise. Baselines are restricted to the residual-based method [55]; no comparison against a marginal-likelihood/nested-sampling estimator is provided (even if expensive), so the practical advantage is asserted rather than directly demonstrated on the same task.

The OOD detection procedure is not fully unsupervised in the strict sense: the test threshold is set from the 95th percentile over a labeled in-distribution reference dataset (FFHQ subset / 50 brain scans). This introduces a dependence on curated ID data that should be stated more explicitly as a requirement, and its sensitivity to the reference set is not analyzed.

The posterior-based rule Φ2 depends on embeddings (LPIPS) that are themselves trained on natural images. The MRI results show this degrades performance (and can favor the wrong model), which raises concerns about the objectivity/robustness of the rule across domains; the paper acknowledges this but the embedding choice appears to materially affect conclusions.

Key hyperparameters (α, K, N, embedding) are chosen heuristically per experiment, and the theoretical trade-offs are only characterized in the tractable Gaussian case. There is little guidance for practitioners on selecting α or diagnosing when the estimator has converged in realistic settings, and SM Fig. 11 shows slow convergence.

Statistical evidence is based on relatively small test sets (60/90 natural images, 50/50 MRI), and the reported accuracy/power numbers carry non-trivial uncertainty; the paper does not report confidence intervals or variability across splits/seeds for the main selection accuracies.

The main text lacks an explicit limitations section; the Discussion is largely a positive summary, with limitations and failure modes relegated to the SM. Some claims (e.g., 'excellent selection and detection accuracy' and 'low computational cost') would benefit from quantitative cost/accuracy comparisons against alternatives.

strengths: Proposes a novel and practical unsupervised framework for Bayesian model selection and misspecification detection in imaging inverse problems, using only a single noisy measurement via data fission and Bayesian cross-validation.
The method is agnostic to the Bayesian sampler and prior, and is compatible with modern implicit priors (plug-and-play, diffusion), which is important for computational imaging.
Establishes a theoretical connection to posterior predictive checks and marginal likelihood; Proposition 1 shows that a specific estimator recovers the marginal likelihood as alpha -> 0.
Introduces two complementary scoring rules (likelihood-based and posterior/embedding-based) that target different aspects of model misspecification.

Provides extensive empirical validation: Gaussian toy analysis, blur-kernel selection, OOD detection for diffusion priors on natural images, MRI reconstruction, Poisson noise, comparison with ProxNest and residual baselines, embedding ablation, and robustness to sample degradation.

Achieves strong empirical performance: 86.7% single-shot and 100% few-shot kernel selection, near-nominal Type I error and high power in OOD tests, and correct model rankings in comparison to nested sampling.
Demonstrates computational efficiency relative to nested sampling/evidence estimation, with runtime analysis and discussion of trade-offs.
Includes implementation details, algorithms, supplementary analyses, and code/data availability (though anonymized), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantee (Proposition 1) applies to the estimator phi^3 = p(y+|x), not directly to the recommended practical estimators Phi^1 (expected log-likelihood) and Phi^2 (posterior discrepancy); the link to marginal likelihood for Phi^1 is only via Jensen's inequality, so finite-alpha behavior lacks rigorous justification.
The posterior-based rule depends heavily on the choice of embedding; CLIP yields poor results and Dreamsim increases Type I error, yet no principled selection procedure is provided.
The method relies on accurate posterior sampling; when the sampler degrades or fails (e.g., too few diffusion steps), the estimators can fail catastrophically, as acknowledged in the appendix.

Computational cost, while lower than nested sampling, remains high for large diffusion models (e.g., ~1802s per image for DiffPIR deblurring), which may limit scalability to large datasets or 3D imaging.

Direct comparisons are limited: only kernel selection is benchmarked against existing residual-based model selection methods, while OOD detection lacks comparison to relevant diffusion-based OOD methods.
Data fission requires knowledge/assumption of the noise model and its parameters (e.g., Gaussian covariance, Poisson gamma); sensitivity to noise misspecification is not extensively studied.
The OOD detection threshold is calibrated on a reference dataset, which may not be available in a fully unsupervised deployment, and the paper assumes such data for setting the 95th percentile.

Presentation issues: Eq. (3) contains a typo (both f^+ and f^- defined as f_alpha^-?), code/data links appear blank (likely anonymized), and there are notation inconsistencies (Phi vs Phi-hat, alpha vs o).

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and under-explored problem: objective (unsupervised) Bayesian model selection and misspecification diagnosis in imaging, using only a single noisy measurement and remaining compatible with implicit deep-learning priors (PnP Langevin, DiffPIR) that cannot be handled by marginal-likelihood or nested-sampling machinery.

The core methodological idea is novel and elegant: combining data fission / measurement splitting with Bayesian cross-validation to obtain a self-supervising predictive-evaluation procedure from a single observation, with alpha trading evaluation accuracy against computational cost.

Provides a useful theoretical anchor: Proposition 1 shows that, for a specific scoring rule, the estimator recovers the marginal likelihood as alpha -> 0, giving a principled interpretation of the approach as a tractable relaxation of evidence computation (with an honest, complete proof in Appendix C.3).

Broad and diverse empirical validation: blur-kernel (likelihood) selection with a PnP Langevin sampler; prior selection and OOD detection with diffusion (DiffPIR) priors on natural images; single-coil MRI at acceleration factors 4 and 8; and Poisson-noise adaptation, plus ablations over alpha, embeddings, sample quality, and number of steps.

Concrete, quantified gains over baselines: 86.7% single-shot and 100% few-shot kernel-selection accuracy versus ~40-60% for residual-based baselines (Vidal et al.), and agreement of the proposed rankings with ProxNest log-evidence and supervised PSNR in the galaxy-denoising study.
Reproducibility is reasonable: pseudo-code is provided (Algorithm 1), computational costs are reported (Table 4), and code/models/ground-truth images are stated to be released.
Presentation is generally clear, with helpful schematic and qualitative figures that make the splitting mechanism and the OOD behavior intuitive.
weaknesses: Disconnect between the theoretical framing and the method that actually drives the strongest results. The proper-scoring-rule framework (Eq. 2) and the marginal-likelihood result (Prop. 1) apply to the likelihood-based rule Phi_1, but the paper itself shows Phi_1 has 'limited value' for OOD detection; the workhorse metric Phi_2 is a posterior-discrepancy heuristic that is not a proper scoring rule and is not covered by the marginal-likelihood theory. The abstract's claim of using 'various scoring rules' is therefore loose.

The bias induced by data fission is not fully characterized for the actual imaging experiments. The construction in Eq. (3) yields synthetic measurements with inflated noise (y+ has covariance Sigma/(1-alpha), y- has Sigma/alpha), so the estimators are biased for alpha > 0; the bias is analyzed only in the Gaussian toy model (Figs. 2-3, Appendix C), whereas the imaging experiments use alpha in {0.1, 0.25, 0.5} and rely on averaging over K realizations to control it.

Limited baselines. There is no comparison to the most closely related unsupervised OOD method (Shoushtari et al., 2025), which the paper itself cites as the nearest prior work, and model-selection comparison is restricted to the residual-based method of Vidal et al. (2021).

Evaluation is small-scale and the headline 'excellent accuracy' is somewhat overstated. Kernel selection is based on only 3 images x 5 kernels (15 experiments, 2 failures), and the 'few shot' setting assumes a shared blur kernel across images, which is a different problem. OOD detection uses 15-90 images, moderate-OOD power is only 60-87%, and the method fails at high blur; thresholds are set at the 95th percentile of a reference set, requiring in-distribution reference data whose absence is not discussed.

The mechanism underlying the OOD signal (divergence of posterior samples under a misspecified prior) may largely re-detect the well-known hallucination behavior of diffusion priors rather than constitute a principled measure of model misspecification, which weakens the novelty/significance of the OOD-detection contribution.

Some minor technical/presentational issues: Eq. (3) contains a typo (both splits labeled f_alpha^-), the posterior-based rule is sensitive to the embedding choice (CLIP essentially fails; Dreamsim yields high Type I error), and the ProxNest validation in Table 5 compares models (WAV, DnCNN, DRUNet) that differ so obviously in quality that the agreement is weak evidence.

strengths: The paper introduces a novel and practically relevant framework for unsupervised Bayesian model selection and misspecification testing in imaging inverse problems, using data fission to create synthetic cross-validation splits from a single noisy measurement.
The method is compatible with modern Bayesian imaging samplers, including plug-and-play Langevin and diffusion-based samplers such as DiffPIR, making it applicable to data-driven priors.

The theoretical connection to posterior predictive checks and the marginal likelihood is insightful; Proposition 1 establishes that the likelihood-scoring estimator recovers the marginal likelihood as alpha tends to 0, with a proof in the appendix.

The proposed likelihood-based and posterior/perceptual-based scoring rules are simple to implement and flexible; experiments demonstrate their utility for likelihood/kernel selection and prior out-of-distribution detection.

The empirical evaluation is broad: toy Gaussian analysis, blur-kernel selection, natural-image OOD detection, MRI reconstruction, Poisson noise, comparison with proximal nested sampling and residual baselines, and ablations over alpha, embeddings, and sample quality.

The method is shown to be computationally cheaper than nested sampling and remains functional even with degraded samples, with detailed implementation and reproducibility information in the supplementary material.
The paper addresses an important open problem in computational imaging: objective model evaluation without ground truth when using highly informative, potentially improper priors.
weaknesses: Theoretical guarantees are limited: Proposition 1 applies to the estimator Phi^3 with likelihood scoring p(y+|x), but the recommended estimators Phi^1 and Phi^2 are not covered. Phi^1 is only Jensen-related to log p(y+|y-), and Phi^2 is a heuristic posterior-sample discrepancy rather than a proper scoring rule. Finite-alpha bias is only characterized in a toy Gaussian setting.

The data-fission splitting assumes a correctly specified noise model, e.g., known Gaussian covariance or exponential-family form. The paper does not evaluate robustness when the noise model is misspecified or its parameters are unknown, despite claiming misspecification testing broadly.

OOD detection requires a reference in-distribution dataset to calibrate the threshold, e.g., 95th percentile, so it is not fully single-measurement or fully unsupervised. The test statistic is also sensitive to the choice of perceptual embedding: CLIP performs poorly, and Dreamsim has high Type I error.

Computational cost, while lower than nested sampling, remains substantial for diffusion models, e.g., 1802 s per image in Table 4. There is no principled automatic way to choose alpha; the tradeoff between accuracy and cost is left to manual tuning.

The model-selection experiments use relatively small test sets, e.g., three images and five kernels, and main tables lack uncertainty estimates or statistical tests. Some baselines may be older or not fully optimized for the compared settings.

Presentation contains several notation errors, e.g., Eq. (3) defines both y+ and y- via f_alpha^-, and Eq. (2) uses an incorrect scoring-rule notation, along with typos such as 'renoise'. The code/data links in the manuscript are blank, which hinders reproducibility if not an artifact of anonymization.

The limitations discussion, while honest, omits key practical caveats: dependence on correct noise splitting, need for reference data, sensitivity to embeddings, and lack of theory for the recommended estimators. The method can also fail catastrophically when the posterior sampler breaks down.
